items.gloss_md: Spectroscopy that measures the resonance frequencies of nuclear spins in a strong magnetic field.
items.body_md: NMR exploits nuclear spin: in a static field B0 the spin states split in energy (Zeeman splitting) and transitions are induced by radiofrequency radiation. Because electronic shielding shifts each nucleus's resonance slightly, NMR is a precise frequency measurement whose small shifts encode chemistry. For metabolomics it is highly reproducible, quantitative, non-destructive and needs minimal sample preparation. Its weaknesses are low sensitivity (about µM–mM), severe signal overlap in 1D ¹H spectra and expensive high-field instruments.

items.gloss_md: The spin quantum number I of a nucleus; only nuclei with I ≠ 0 have a magnetic moment and are NMR-observable.
items.body_md: A nucleus with spin quantum number I has angular momentum P = √(I(I+1))·ħ and magnetic moment μ = γ·P, where γ is the isotope-specific gyromagnetic ratio. Nuclei with even numbers of both protons and neutrons (e.g. ¹²C, ¹⁶O) have I = 0 and are invisible to NMR. ¹H and ¹³C have I = ½; ²H and ¹⁴N have I = 1. In a field B0 the z-component is quantized (m = −I,…,+I); a spin-½ nucleus has two states split in energy (Zeeman splitting).

items.gloss_md: The resonance frequency ν0 = γ·B0/(2π) at which RF radiation induces spin transitions.
items.body_md: For spin-½ the energy gap is ΔE = γ·ħ·B0 = hν0. At 14.1 T, ¹H resonates near 600 MHz, hence a '600 MHz spectrometer'. The field a nucleus actually experiences is reduced by electronic shielding, B_eff = B0(1 − σ), so chemically inequivalent nuclei resonate at slightly different frequencies.

items.gloss_md: Resonance position relative to a reference, δ = (ν_sample − ν_ref)/ν_ref × 10⁶, in ppm.
items.body_md: Dividing by the spectrometer frequency makes δ field-independent, so spectra from different magnets are directly comparable (J-couplings, in contrast, are constant in Hz). In aqueous metabolomics the reference set to 0 ppm is TSP or DSS, whose 9 equivalent protons give one sharp line. The ¹H chemical-shift range is narrow (~10 ppm), a main cause of signal overlap in biofluids; ¹³C spans >200 ppm.

items.gloss_md: NMR is intrinsically insensitive because the signal comes from a tiny Boltzmann population difference.
items.body_md: ΔN/N ≈ γħB0/(2kT), only about 1 in 10⁴–10⁵ at room temperature, so only a small net excess contributes to the magnetization. Sensitivity improves with higher B0, cryoprobes, microprobes, signal averaging (S/N ∝ √n) and methods like dynamic nuclear polarization. Higher B0 also improves resolution, because shifts in Hz scale with B0 while J-couplings stay fixed; the cost is very expensive magnets.

items.gloss_md: NMR of hydrogen nuclei, the workhorse of NMR-based metabolomics.
items.body_md: ¹H combines high gyromagnetic ratio and ~100% natural abundance, and nearly all metabolites contain hydrogen, so one 1D ¹H experiment profiles most of the metabolome quickly. Its drawback is the narrow ~10 ppm shift range, causing extensive overlap. ¹³C (1.1% abundance), ³¹P (few metabolites contain P) and ¹⁵N (0.37% abundance) trade sensitivity or coverage for dispersion.

items.gloss_md: Longitudinal relaxation restoring the z-magnetization by exchanging energy with the surroundings.
items.body_md: T1 relaxation restores the Boltzmann population difference after an RF pulse. It sets how long one must wait between scans to avoid saturation. For quantitative NMR the relaxation delay plus acquisition should be at least about 5·T1, otherwise long-T1 protons are under-counted.

items.gloss_md: Transverse relaxation: decay of xy-magnetization as spins lose phase coherence; it governs linewidth.
items.body_md: T2 relaxation needs no net energy exchange. The FID decays as exp(−t/T2), and a shorter T2 gives a broader line. The observed decay constant T2* also includes dephasing from field inhomogeneity, so linewidths are usually broader than the natural 1/(πT2). Large, slowly tumbling molecules have short T2 and broad signals.

items.gloss_md: The raw time-domain NMR signal: an oscillation at the Larmor frequency decaying as exp(−t/T2*).
items.body_md: The FID is what the spectrometer acquires; Fourier transformation turns it into the frequency-domain spectrum. Before the transform it is typically apodized (window function) and zero-filled.

items.gloss_md: The peak shape of a liquid-state NMR signal: f(ω) = A·λ/((ω−ω0)² + λ²).
items.body_md: The Fourier transform of an exponentially decaying cosine (the FID) is exactly a Lorentzian centred at the resonance frequency, with FWHM Δν = 1/(π·T2*). In the metabodeconplus parameterization ω0 is the centre, λ the half-width at half-maximum and A an amplitude factor; the integral is πA and the peak height A/λ. Field inhomogeneity can add a Gaussian component (Voigt profile). This is the mechanistic justification for modelling metabolite signals as Lorentzians in deconvolution.

items.gloss_md: Factors that shorten T2* and widen NMR peaks, causing overlap in crowded spectra.
items.body_md: Contributors are intrinsic T2 relaxation (faster for large, slowly tumbling molecules), magnetic-field inhomogeneity (poor shimming), chemical exchange, sample viscosity and molecular interactions, and the measurement/processing itself. Together with the narrow ¹H shift range and hundreds of metabolites, these linewidths make peaks in urine and plasma overlap. Chemical exchange (e.g. labile OH/NH protons exchanging with water, or titrating metabolites) broadens lines in the intermediate regime and makes signals pH-dependent, stressing both deconvolution and alignment.

items.gloss_md: Co-located peaks within one NMR spectrum that cannot be read off individually.
items.body_md: In 1D ¹H spectra of biofluids, the narrow ~10 ppm range, hundreds of metabolites and finite linewidths cause extensive overlap. Overlap is a within-spectrum problem solved by deconvolution (or by 2D NMR), distinct from chemical-shift drift across spectra.

items.gloss_md: Small sample-to-sample shifts in a metabolite's peak positions caused by pH, temperature and ionic strength.
items.body_md: The same metabolite's resonance moves with pH (especially titratable metabolites like citrate, histidine), temperature, ionic strength and solvent composition. Drift is about matching the same peak across spectra (an alignment problem), whereas overlap is about resolving peaks within one spectrum. Without correction one metabolite's intensity lands in different feature columns, corrupting statistical comparisons.

items.gloss_md: Under full relaxation, the integrated ¹H signal area is proportional to the number of protons.
items.body_md: Because all ¹H nuclei respond identically, one internal standard of known concentration (e.g. TSP) calibrates the entire spectrum without compound-specific response factors, a major advantage over MS. The condition is that spins relax essentially fully between scans (relaxation delay + acquisition ≥ about 5·T1); otherwise long-T1 signals are attenuated.

items.gloss_md: Splitting of a signal into a multiplet by neighbouring protons, constant in Hz.
items.body_md: Protons on neighbouring carbons split each other's signals into doublets, triplets, … following the n+1 rule. Together with chemically inequivalent proton groups, this gives each metabolite a characteristic pattern of several peaks. A deconvolution tool that treats peaks independently (as metabodeconplus does, without multiplet grouping) produces several correlated features per metabolite.

items.gloss_md: Removing the huge water resonance in biofluid ¹H NMR, typically by presaturation.
items.body_md: Water protons (~55 M) exceed metabolites by 10⁴–10⁵ and would dominate the receiver and swamp metabolite signals. Presaturation applies a weak selective RF field at the water frequency during the relaxation delay, saturating water spins while off-resonance metabolites are largely unaffected; it underlies 1D NOESY-presat. Downsides: exchangeable protons near water are attenuated and a residual hump may remain. Urine spectra are typically acquired with 1D NOESY-presat for its robust water suppression and flat baseline.

items.gloss_md: Carr–Purcell–Meiboom–Gill spin-echo train acting as a T2 filter; used for plasma/serum.
items.body_md: Plasma contains proteins and lipoproteins with very short T2 that form a broad rolling background. During the CPMG echo period this fast-decaying macromolecule magnetization dies away while sharp small-metabolite signals (long T2) survive, giving a clean spectrum on a flat baseline. Urine lacks this background and is measured with 1D NOESY-presat instead.

items.gloss_md: NMR experiments (COSY, TOCSY, HSQC, HMBC) that spread signals over a second frequency axis.
items.body_md: COSY shows ¹H–¹H cross-peaks between directly J-coupled protons; TOCSY correlates a whole coupled spin system; HSQC gives one-bond ¹H–¹³C correlations; HMBC gives 2–3-bond ¹H–¹³C correlations. They resolve overlap and aid assignment, but cost much more acquisition time, produce larger data and are harder to quantify at cohort scale. So 1D ¹H with computational deconvolution remains the default in metabolomics.

items.gloss_md: Adjusting auxiliary coil currents to make B0 as homogeneous as possible over the sample.
items.body_md: Field inhomogeneity dephases spins (shortens T2*) and broadens and distorts lines. Good shimming gives sharp, symmetric, truly Lorentzian peaks and a flat baseline, improving resolution and the validity of Lorentzian deconvolution. The lock channel monitors the ²H resonance of a deuterated solvent (e.g. D2O) and adjusts B0 to correct slow field drift.

items.gloss_md: NMR of intact tissue spun at 54.74° to B0 to average out anisotropic line broadening.
items.body_md: In solids and semi-solids, dipolar couplings, chemical-shift anisotropy and susceptibility effects broaden lines; these scale with (3cos²θ − 1), which is zero at 54.74°. Fast spinning at that angle recovers near-solution linewidths. It is used for intact tissue biopsies, while solution-state NMR remains the choice for liquid biofluids.

items.gloss_md: Analytical technique that ionises analytes and separates them by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).
items.body_md: In metabolomics MS is very sensitive and selective with wide coverage, usually after LC or GC separation. Weaknesses: often destructive, ionization efficiency varies so quantification needs compound-specific standards, ion-suppression/matrix effects, narrower dynamic range and lower reproducibility across labs than NMR. Targeted MS uses multiple-reaction monitoring with stable-isotope-labelled internal standards. NMR and MS are complementary.

items.gloss_md: The complete set of small-molecule metabolites; the molecular layer considered closest to the phenotype.
items.body_md: The metabolome lies downstream of genome, transcriptome and proteome and integrates gene expression, enzyme activity and environmental inputs (diet, drugs, microbiome, disease). It therefore reflects the organism's actual physiological state and suits biomarker discovery. Caveats: signatures capture correlation not causation, and the metabolome is dynamic and influenced by many confounders, so data are noisy.

items.gloss_md: The large-scale measurement and analysis of metabolites, mainly by NMR and mass spectrometry.
items.body_md: NMR and MS are the two main, complementary platforms: NMR is reproducible and quantitative but insensitive; MS is sensitive with wide coverage but less reproducible and harder to quantify. Results feed biomarker discovery, disease-risk assessment and pathway analysis.

items.gloss_md: The standard steps from raw FID to statistical analysis in NMR metabolomics.
items.body_md: Steps: acquisition (FID); apodization and zero-filling; Fourier transformation; phase and baseline correction; chemical-shift referencing (TSP/DSS) and water-region removal; feature extraction by binning or deconvolution; alignment across samples; normalization (e.g. total area or creatinine for urine) and scaling; optional annotation; statistical analysis (PCA, PLS-DA, random forests).

items.gloss_md: Fingerprinting approach that models all resolved signals without requiring prior metabolite annotation.
items.body_md: Statistics run directly on resolved signals (peaks or bins), so signals of unknown origin can still be discriminatory biomarkers; important ones are annotated afterwards. Targeted profiling instead quantifies a predefined list of known metabolites. Since only a small fraction of signals can be confidently annotated (much of the metabolome is 'dark matter'), untargeted approaches lose no information to incomplete libraries.

items.gloss_md: Metabolomics Standards Initiative levels; level 1 needs two orthogonal properties matched to an authentic standard.
items.body_md: Defined by Sumner et al. 2007, the gold standard (level 1) matches e.g. retention time and mass spectrum to an authentic standard measured under identical conditions. A database lookup by mass or shift yields only candidates (putative annotation). A meta-analysis (Kodra et al. 2022) found only about 20% of papers reached level 1; the bottleneck is the cost and availability of standards, which motivates RT prediction and spectral libraries.

items.gloss_md: Feature extraction that sums spectral intensity within fixed or adaptive chemical-shift intervals.
items.body_md: Binning is simple, fast, robust to noise and tolerant of small peak shifts, and needs no peak model. Its principal disadvantage is that one bin can mix several overlapping peaks or metabolites, so a discriminatory bin cannot be attributed to one metabolite. On the AKI cohort a 700-bin baseline (0.01 ppm bins) matched metabodeconplus in accuracy, but without per-peak interpretability.

items.gloss_md: Decomposing an overlapped NMR spectrum into individual (Lorentzian) peaks with positions and integrals.
items.body_md: Because signals overlap in 1D ¹H biofluid spectra, individual peaks must be resolved computationally by fitting a superposition of Lorentzians. Peak-based features are localised, each contributing to a single metabolite, unlike bins. Classical curve fitting uses least squares (e.g. Levenberg–Marquardt); Koh's approach is analytic and derivative-free.

items.gloss_md: R package unifying NMR deconvolution, cross-sample alignment, feature-matrix construction and random-forest classification.
items.body_md: It is not a new version of MetaboDecon1D but a broader package with automated parameter optimization and a fast Rust backend, scaling to several hundred spectra. It quantifies every resolvable peak whether or not its metabolite is known. On the AKI urine cohort it matched a binning baseline in accuracy and AUC while giving interpretable per-peak features. Limitations: native readers only for Bruker and JCAMP-DX, no multiplet grouping, no automatic peak-to-metabolite assignment, and an expensive supervised 3-D parameter search. An optional Rust backend (mdrb, via use_rust) gives very close but not identical results and makes grid search fast; work is parallelized across spectra, not grid rows, to save memory.

items.gloss_md: Predecessor tool implementing Koh's two-stage curvature-based detection and analytic Lorentzian approximation.
items.body_md: Koh et al. (2008/2009) identify peaks as negative local minima of the second derivative S'', filter them by a noise-based score, and approximate each peak analytically as a Lorentzian with iterative proportional rescaling. Unlike Levenberg–Marquardt it needs no partial derivatives and its runtime is essentially independent of the number of data points. MetaboDecon1D deconvoluted single spectra only (~40 s at 2¹⁷ points) and fitted Lorentzians to smoothed intensities, which biased narrow peaks.

items.gloss_md: Detecting peaks as local minima of the second derivative of the smoothed spectrum.
items.body_md: Each peak is a triplet of points (left, centre, right) and is scored by the minimum of the cumulative |S''| sums over its left and right halves, so sharp peaks score high. A small peak fully shadowed by a larger neighbour has no curvature minimum of its own and cannot be detected. Detection runs on a moving-average-smoothed spectrum (window smws, iterations smit), but metabodeconplus fits Lorentzians to raw intensities because smoothing lowers and broadens narrow peaks. Peaks are kept only if their score exceeds μ + δ·σ of the noise-region score distribution: δ too low admits noise peaks, δ too high misses weak signals (default 6.4).

items.gloss_md: Closed-form Lorentzian parameters from three peak points, then proportional rescaling to fit the spectrum.
items.body_md: Substituting three observed points into y = A·λ/((ω−ω0)²+λ²) gives a closed-form ω0, then λ² and A·λ. To avoid dividing by y1 − y3 (near zero for symmetric peaks), λ² is computed from the inner pairs and averaged. Because neighbouring peaks overlap, the superposition of independent estimates overshoots the spectrum; Koh's rule of proportion rescales each peak by observed/reconstructed intensity over nfit passes.

items.gloss_md: Reconstruction error AR = Σ|y − ŷ| / Σ|y| between observed spectrum and Lorentzian superposition.
items.body_md: AR is the unsupervised objective for per-spectrum parameter optimization. It keeps decreasing as more Lorentzians are added, so minimizing it alone over-fits with spurious peaks; a peak ceiling npmax is required. On noisy spectra AR stays above 0 even with every true peak recovered.

items.gloss_md: Maximum expected number of peaks per spectrum; the critical user-set parameter of metabodeconplus.
items.body_md: The optimizer picks the smallest-AR grid cell (smit, smws, delta, nfit = 10) whose peak count does not exceed npmax. Too low excludes genuine peaks; too high fits noise. It is chosen from domain knowledge (urine has more peaks than plasma; npmax = 1000 for the AKI urine cohort), visual inspection, or downstream classification performance.

items.gloss_md: Automated choice of nfit, smit, smws, delta (unsupervised) and npmax, maxShift, maxCombine (supervised).
items.body_md: Unsupervised: per spectrum, minimize AR subject to npmax over a 60-cell grid. Supervised: score parameter combinations by random-forest out-of-bag error. A full npmax × maxShift × maxCombine grid is expensive, so the recommendation is to fix npmax, let CluPA self-tune maxShift (−1) and sweep only maxCombine. fit_mdm() caches per-npmax parameters, reuses deconvolution and alignment between grid rows, and parallelizes over spectra.

items.gloss_md: Samples × aligned-peak table of integrals used for statistics and classification.
items.body_md: In metabodeconplus each column is one aligned Lorentzian peak, so a discriminatory feature can be assigned to a single metabolite and transferred to targeted assays. The matrix is sparse with structural zeros: a zero means 'peak missing', not 'area measured as zero', which linear models confound.

items.gloss_md: Ensemble of decision trees on bootstrap samples; used (ranger) as metabodeconplus's classifier.
items.body_md: Being non-linear, a random forest can split on presence/absence as well as magnitude, so it handles the 'missing peak vs small area' zeros of the feature matrix that destabilize linear models. In the AKI benchmark the same ranger forest (probability mode) was used for both binning and peak features for a fair comparison. Its out-of-bag (OOB) error, computed from each tree's predictions on samples outside its bootstrap sample, lets metabodeconplus score parameter combinations without a held-out split or inner cross-validation.

items.gloss_md: Matching corresponding peaks across spectra onto a common grid to correct chemical-shift drift.
items.body_md: Needed after deconvolution because the same metabolite drifts with pH, temperature and ionic strength. metabodeconplus aligns peak lists (not raw spectra) in two steps: CluPA for coarse segment shifts, then snap_to_ref for fine per-peak correction. Aligning to a fixed reference makes the procedure reproducible and extensible: new samples are aligned to the same reference without recomputing the cohort.

items.gloss_md: Hierarchical cluster-based alignment shifting spectral segments by FFT cross-correlation.
items.body_md: From speaq (Vu et al.): after a global shift, segments defined by hierarchical clustering of the combined reference + target peak list are bisected recursively. Each segment gets an integer-datapoint shift from FFT cross-correlation bounded by maxShift; recursion stops when a segment has peaks from one spectrum only or fewer than three peaks. Because all peaks in a segment move together, peaks are not guaranteed an exact common shift. maxShift = −1 doubles maxShift (1, 2, 4, …) and stops one step before the average pairwise Pearson correlation first decreases.

items.gloss_md: Snaps each remaining peak to the nearest reference peak column within maxCombine.
items.body_md: It enforces a truly common peak grid after CluPA; maxCombine is the residual positional uncertainty after CluPA. Peaks farther than maxCombine from every reference peak are dropped, so rare peaks can be lost. Too small a window fails correct snaps; too large on crowded spectra lets wrong neighbouring peaks intrude.

items.gloss_md: Deconvolution quality metric PRX·(1 − AR) combining correct peak recovery and reconstruction fidelity.
items.body_md: PRX = c/(t + i) (correct peaks over true plus incorrect peaks); AR = residual over observed signal. AR alone rewards over-fitting and the plain peak ratio ignores wrong detections; their product needs both. It requires ground-truth peaks (simulations or spiked controls) and cannot reach 1 on noisy spectra: the noise floor keeps AR > 0 and shadowed peaks keep PRX < 1.

items.gloss_md: 100 simulated plasma-like spectra with 25 known Lorentzian peaks and 3 discriminating peaks.
items.body_md: 2048 points over 3.59–3.28 ppm, groups A/B 50/50, peaks derived from a deconvolution of real blood plasma. Perturbations: global ppm shift, per-peak jitter, amplitude scaling U[0.4,1.6], half-width scaling U[0.9,1.1] and Gaussian noise. In group A three peaks are scaled by 1.25, 1.25 and 1/1.25, a known moderate class signal; the first spectrum is the clean reference. Snap purity, the fraction of (spectrum, true peak) pairs whose reference column holds the correct peak and no wrong one, measures alignment quality directly on Sim2.

items.gloss_md: 106 urinary ¹H NMR spectra (34 acute kidney injury vs 72 controls) used to benchmark metabodeconplus.
items.body_md: The baseline mirrors Zacharias (2013): 700 fixed 0.01 ppm bins, with the original SVM replaced by the same ranger random forest. metabodeconplus used npmax = 1000, maxShift = −1 and maxCombine swept per training fold; evaluation by stratified 10-fold CV over 3 seeds. Both matched in accuracy and AUC; the peak-based matrix adds interpretability and assay transfer.

items.gloss_md: Learned peak picking/deconvolution such as DEEP Picker1D and Bruker's mldecon, trained on synthetic spectra.
items.body_md: DEEP Picker1D is a CNN with Voigt least-squares refinement; mldecon is part of TopSpin 4.2. They can do well on crowded regions and may infer shadowed peaks from shape priors, but depend on representative training spectra and are less transparent. metabodeconplus is deterministic, training-free and broader in scope (it adds alignment and classification).

items.gloss_md: Tools (BATMAN, ASICS, rDolphin, Chenomx, Bayesil) that fit spectra as combinations of known metabolite spectra.
items.body_md: They can only report metabolites in their library, so unknown or unassigned signals are lost. metabodeconplus instead deconvolutes every resolvable signal, so unidentified peaks still become features.

items.gloss_md: R package and Shiny app that predicts LC retention times from molecular structure.
items.body_md: FastRet supports LC-MS annotation by using predicted RT as an orthogonal filter on candidate identities. It implements three tasks: training from SMILES + measured RTs (Lasso or boosted trees on 241 CDK descriptors), selective measuring, and model adjustment to modified chromatographic conditions. Training and prediction take seconds on one CPU core; it is on CRAN with a web app at fastret.spang-lab.de (tabs Train, Select, Adjust, Predict). It generalises as a method retrained or adjusted per chromatographic system, not as one portable model. Predicted RTs are clipped to a plausible range from a log-normal fit to the training RTs, mainly to contain Lasso's extrapolation failures. From scratch it is competitive with Retip (boosted trees on CDK descriptors) and in low-data transfer it is the strongest structure-based method; on 14 public RepoRT datasets from other labs it reached median R² 0.60 (RP) and 0.58 (HILIC).

items.gloss_md: The time an analyte takes to elute from an LC column; system-specific.
items.body_md: RT depends on stationary-phase chemistry, column dimensions, mobile phase and additives/pH, gradient profile, flow rate, temperature, separation mechanism, and void and dwell volumes, and it drifts as columns age. Unlike accurate mass or MS/MS spectra, RT cannot be looked up in universal databases. In LC-MS it is a second, orthogonal identification dimension next to m/z, but its discriminating power is modest and co-eluting isomers share RT.

items.gloss_md: Computationally predicting an analyte's RT on a given chromatographic system from its structure.
items.body_md: Authentic standards are costly and not always available, and RTs are system-specific, so predicting RTs for unmeasured candidates breaks the identification bottleneck. Candidates whose predicted RT deviates strongly from the observed one are excluded, prioritising candidates without proving identity. Models are tied to one setup and must be retrained or adjusted when conditions change. Approaches include physicochemical models, QSRR, projection/transfer methods (PredRet) and learned representations (GNNs, DeepGCN-RT).

items.gloss_md: Statistical modelling that maps numerical descriptors of molecular structure to retention.
items.body_md: QSRR needs no mechanistic model of chromatography. It works because retention is largely governed by properties that descriptors encode: lipophilicity first, then polar surface area, H-bonding and charge. FastRet is a QSRR method combined with a descriptor-aware adjustment step.

items.gloss_md: Numerical feature computed from a molecule's structure (e.g. from SMILES), such as logP or polar surface area.
items.body_md: FastRet uses 241 CDK descriptors: constitutional, topological, electrotopological and physicochemical (XLogP, ALogP, TopoPSA, H-bond donors/acceptors, rotatable bonds, Kier shape, BCUT, …). Descriptor values are cached by SMILES; rare missing values are mean-imputed and near-zero-variance descriptors (~101) removed. Fitted models are sparse (Lasso kept 15–41 descriptors), dominated by lipophilicity indices on RP data. Descriptor quality is a fundamental limit on model quality.

items.gloss_md: Java cheminformatics library, used in FastRet through the rcdk R wrapper to compute descriptors.
items.body_md: rcdk is the only molecular-descriptor engine callable directly from R (Rcpi delegates to it), so FastRet stays a single, easy-to-install R dependency. PaDEL, Mordred, RDKit and Dragon/alvaDesc need a separate Python or Java toolchain.

items.gloss_md: Linear regression with an L1 penalty that shrinks many coefficients exactly to zero.
items.body_md: The L1 penalty induces sparsity and built-in feature selection, suiting high-dimensional p > n data. FastRet fits it with glmnet, choosing λ by ten-fold CV over 100 values; as a linear model it can extrapolate to extreme predictions outside the training descriptor range. In ADMIRE's MGM the λ‖Θ‖₁ term drives edge weights to zero so only genuine conditional dependencies remain.

items.gloss_md: Gradient-boosted decision trees (xgboost), FastRet's non-linear model family.
items.body_md: BRT weights features by split gain and is robust to correlated and uninformative descriptors. FastRet tunes only nrounds by internal CV with early stopping. BRT outperformed Lasso on larger training sets (test R² 0.86 RP, 0.81 HILIC, 0.66 RP-AXMM) and is more stable, because predictions stay within the training RT range.

items.gloss_md: Estimating generalization by repeatedly fitting on part of the data and testing on the held-out rest.
items.body_md: FastRet uses CV for hyperparameters and performance, but evaluates adjustment with dedicated train/test sets: test compounds must be in neither the base nor the adjustment-training set, which folded CV would make complex. In FastRet, inner CV selects λ (Lasso) or nrounds (BRT) and an outer CV estimates performance, i.e. nested cross-validation.

items.gloss_md: Choosing the k most informative compounds to measure on a new LC setup under a limited budget.
items.body_md: Step 1: Ridge regression of RT on descriptors weights the features. Step 2: k-medoids (PAM) clustering in the weighted descriptor + RT space, measuring one medoid per cluster. Variants differ in RT weight: SM0 (none), SM1 (unchanged), SMmax (scaled to the largest Ridge coefficient), SMinf (RT only). SMmax is recommended with model adjustment; all variants give narrower R² distributions than random selection.

items.gloss_md: Linear regression with an L2 penalty that shrinks coefficients without zeroing them.
items.body_md: FastRet's selective measuring uses Ridge rather than Lasso for feature weighting because, under a different chromatographic condition, the informative features may change; zeroing features too early would be premature.

items.gloss_md: Clustering whose cluster centres are actual data points (medoids).
items.body_md: Partitioning Around Medoids (R cluster package) is used in selective measuring because each medoid is a real compound that can be ordered and measured, whereas k-means centres generally correspond to no molecule.

items.gloss_md: Adapting an existing RT model to modified chromatographic conditions from a few re-measured compounds.
items.body_md: FastRet's adjustment predicts the new RT from the base RT together with descriptors, and uses a predicted (not measured) base RT, so it covers compounds never measured on the original system. Descriptor-aware adjustment helps most when the setup change alters the retention mechanism (RP → RP-AXMM, r = 0.797). With ~25 compounds a Lasso adjustment on a BRT base model is recommended; it approached from-scratch performance, and on 22 unseen validation metabolites reached R² ≈ 0.81–0.84.

items.gloss_md: Mapping RTs from one chromatographic system to another using RT as the only input (e.g. PredRet).
items.body_md: Projection methods (PredRet, Osipenko, Zhang) learn an RT-to-RT mapping, e.g. a monotone spline. Their core limitation: a molecule never measured on the source system has no base RT and is out of scope. A PredRet-like baseline helps only on highly correlated RP pairs.

items.gloss_md: logP: logarithm of the octanol–water partition coefficient, a measure of how lipophilic a compound is.
items.body_md: Reversed-phase retention is a partitioning process analogous to octanol–water partition, so higher-logP compounds are retained longer and log k correlates near-linearly with logP. Lipophilicity indices (XLogP, ALogP) dominate FastRet's RP models.

items.gloss_md: Separation by differential distribution of analytes between a stationary phase and a flowing liquid mobile phase.
items.body_md: Compounds interacting more with the stationary phase are retarded more and elute later. Separation combines thermodynamics (retention) with kinetic band broadening that limits resolution. In LC-MS the column provides the time-resolved first dimension and the mass spectrometer the mass-resolved second.

items.gloss_md: k = (t_R − t_0)/t_0: time in the stationary phase relative to time in the mobile phase.
items.body_md: Equivalently k = K·(V_s/V_m). Under isocratic conditions k is independent of flow rate and column dimensions, so it is the transferable quantity; raising flow rate lowers t_R but leaves k unchanged. Useful values are roughly 1–10; k ≈ 0 means co-elution with the void.

items.gloss_md: t_0 = V_0/flow: time for an unretained solute to traverse the column system's void volume.
items.body_md: The void volume is the mobile-phase volume not occupied by stationary phase, including extra-column tubing. t_0 sets the earliest elution and is needed to convert RT to k. Void volume is one system-specific factor making raw RTs non-transferable between instruments.

items.gloss_md: How well two peaks are separated, combining spacing and width; Rs ≈ 1.5 is baseline separation.
items.body_md: The resolution equation has three multiplicative terms: efficiency (√N/4), selectivity ((α−1)/α) and retention (k/(1+k)). Increasing N has square-root returns and raises backpressure; increasing k helps until it plateaus. Selectivity α = k₂/k₁ is usually the most powerful lever; α = 1 means no separation is possible.

items.gloss_md: H = A + B/u + C·u: plate height versus linear mobile-phase velocity.
items.body_md: A is eddy diffusion (multiple flow paths), B longitudinal diffusion (dominant at low velocity), C resistance to mass transfer (dominant at high velocity, scales with particle diameter squared). Smaller particles shrink A and especially C and flatten the curve, enabling fast UHPLC at the cost of backpressure ∝ 1/d_p². Flow rate thus trades efficiency between B- and C-term broadening.

items.gloss_md: N = (t_R/σ)² measures column efficiency; HETP H = L/N normalizes it per column length.
items.body_md: Common forms are N = 16·(t_R/w)² or 5.54·(t_R/w_1/2)². Higher N means sharper peaks; smaller H is better. N grows with column length and smaller, well-packed particles. It is an isocratic concept; for gradients peak capacity is more relevant.

items.gloss_md: The maximum number of peaks that fit side by side at a given resolution within the retention window.
items.body_md: It is the figure of merit for gradient elution, where peaks are compressed to similar widths. n_c ≈ 1 + t_gradient/average peak width; it rises with longer/shallower gradients and more efficient columns. For complex metabolomics samples it reduces co-elution and ion suppression.

items.gloss_md: LC with a non-polar stationary phase (C18/C8) and a polar aqueous–organic mobile phase.
items.body_md: Retention is driven by hydrophobic (solvophobic) interaction, so polar compounds elute early and lipophilic ones late; retention correlates with logP. Increasing the organic modifier (%B) decreases retention roughly log-linearly (log k ≈ log k_w − S·φ), so RP gradients increase %B over time. T3 phases (e.g. HSS T3) resist phase collapse in 100% aqueous mobile phase and retain polar compounds better. In FastRet, RP was the easiest mode to predict (R² ≈ 0.86).

items.gloss_md: LC with a polar stationary phase and a high-organic mobile phase that retains polar compounds.
items.body_md: Polar analytes partition into a water-enriched layer on the stationary phase, plus adsorption and electrostatic contributions. Elution order is the reverse of RP, and the gradient increases the aqueous fraction. RP and HILIC are orthogonal and complementary, so comprehensive metabolomics often needs both. HILIC needs long equilibration and is sensitive to water content, buffer, pH and sample solvent, making RTs less reproducible (FastRet R² ≈ 0.81).

items.gloss_md: A stationary phase combining hydrophobic C18 and charged anion-exchange retention mechanisms.
items.body_md: Retention is the sum of a hydrophobic and an electrostatic contribution, tunable by pH, ionic strength and salt. It can retain both hydrophobic and charged polar compounds in one run, but retention is harder to predict. RP-AXMM was FastRet's hardest mode (R² ≈ 0.66): structure descriptors capture the charge-dependent component poorly and RP-to-RP-AXMM base-RT correlation is weak (r = 0.797).

items.gloss_md: Changing mobile-phase strength during the run, in contrast to constant-composition isocratic elution.
items.body_md: Gradients solve the general elution problem: no single isocratic composition resolves early compounds and elutes strongly retained ones in reasonable time. Steeper gradients shorten runs but reduce peak capacity and resolution; shallower ones spread peaks at the cost of time, and steepness can change selectivity. Costs: re-equilibration, dwell volume and gradient-shape dependence make RTs harder to transfer. The dwell (gradient delay) volume between mixer and column head acts as an initial isocratic hold and differs between instruments, a major source of RT non-transferability.

items.gloss_md: pH sets the charge state of ionisable analytes (via pKa) and so their retention.
items.body_md: In RP the neutral form is retained more; retention changes sharply near pH ≈ pKa, so operating away from pKa gives reproducible retention. pH also affects silanol ionisation and, in mixed-mode, the electrostatic component; it is another setup variable an RT model is tied to. Volatile additives such as formic acid and ammonium formate control pH and ionic strength in LC-MS; non-volatile buffers like phosphate would precipitate in the ESI source.

items.gloss_md: Soft ionisation that turns LC eluent into charged droplets and gas-phase ions for the mass spectrometer.
items.body_md: A high voltage at the capillary tip disperses the liquid; as solvent evaporates, ions such as [M+H]+ or [M−H]− are ejected. ESI produces mostly intact molecular ions but is concentration-sensitive and competitive.

items.gloss_md: Loss (or enhancement) of an analyte's MS signal caused by co-eluting compounds competing for charge.
items.body_md: Co-eluting matrix, salts or additives compete in the electrospray source, harming sensitivity, quantitation and reproducibility. Good chromatographic separation and volatile additives mitigate it; stable-isotope internal standards correct for it.

items.gloss_md: Porous silica particles with bonded ligands (e.g. C18), optionally endcapped or hybrid (BEH).
items.body_md: Ligands are bonded to surface silanols; residual silanols cause tailing for bases, and endcapping masks them with small silanes. Pure silica is limited to roughly pH 2–8. BEH (bridged ethylene hybrid) particles add ethylene bridges for mechanical and pH stability and lower silanol activity.

items.gloss_md: Higher temperature usually lowers retention, viscosity and backpressure and can change selectivity.
items.body_md: Retention vs temperature follows the van 't Hoff relationship: ln k vs 1/T is typically linear with slope −ΔH/R. Lower viscosity speeds mass transfer (C term) and allows higher flow. Because analytes differ in transfer enthalpy, temperature can re-order peaks; FastRet's adjustment experiments varied it (25 vs 35 °C).

items.gloss_md: LC with sub-2 µm particles and very high-pressure instrumentation.
items.body_md: Smaller particles lower plate height and flatten the van Deemter curve, giving faster separations, sharper peaks, higher peak capacity and sensitivity. Backpressure scales with 1/d_p², requiring pumps rated to hundreds to over 1000 bar. The thesis used 1.7–1.8 µm BEH/HSS columns.

items.gloss_md: Peak widening in LC from on-column (van Deemter) and extra-column contributions.
items.body_md: On-column: eddy diffusion, longitudinal diffusion and mass-transfer resistance, plus pore diffusion and non-uniform packing. Extra-column: injector, tubing, unions, frits and detector volumes, especially damaging in UHPLC. Bed voids and overloading also broaden peaks, lowering N, resolution and sensitivity.

items.gloss_md: Particles with a solid core and thin porous shell that shorten diffusion paths.
items.body_md: The thin shell reduces the C term and the narrow size distribution reduces the A term, approaching sub-2 µm efficiency at much lower backpressure (e.g. 2.6–2.7 µm particles). Trade-off: lower surface area and loading capacity.

items.gloss_md: Anomaly Detection using MIxed gRaphical modEls: detects and corrects single erroneous entries in mixed data matrices.
items.body_md: ADMIRE scores each cell against its conditional distribution given all other features of the same sample, rather than flagging whole samples. It jointly models continuous OMICS features and discrete phenotype/design variables, and also corrects flagged values and imputes missing ones. The MGM machinery comes from Altenbuchinger et al. 2019; the anomaly framework, correction, imputation and LOO-CV penalty selection are ADMIRE's contributions. The Python package adadmire is on PyPI (MIT, spang-lab/adadmire) with Sphinx docs and GitHub Actions CI.

items.gloss_md: Finding values inconsistent with the structure of the rest of the data.
items.body_md: An anomaly need not be an error: it can be a rare but genuine observation, so flags are hypotheses requiring domain follow-up. Anomaly detection presumes anomalies are a minority; ADMIRE stayed stable up to ~45% contamination and collapsed from 50%, when the model fits the predominant noise as structure.

items.gloss_md: A value typical for its feature's marginal distribution but atypical given the other features.
items.body_md: An outlier is extreme in its feature's marginal distribution; anomalies are more general, and outliers are a special case. Example: a gene expressed at 4–6 in men and 8–14 in women; 12 in a man is not an outlier but is an anomaly given sex. In the simulation, hidden anomalies lie within the feature's interquartile range; univariate/sample-level methods are blind to them, which is where ADMIRE's advantage is largest.

items.gloss_md: Pairwise Markov random field jointly modelling continuous and discrete variables.
items.body_md: Density p(x,y) ∝ exp(−½Σβ_js x_j x_s + Σα_j x_j + Σρ_js(y_s)x_j + Σφ_js(y_j,y_s)), following Lee & Hastie 2015. It generalizes Gaussian graphical models to mixed data: continuous nodes have Gaussian conditionals with mean α_j + Σρ_js(y_s) − Σβ_js x_s and variance 1/β_jj; discrete nodes have multinomial logistic conditionals. A missing edge encodes conditional independence. Fitting has O((p+q)²) parameters, the main scalability limit for wide OMICS matrices.

items.gloss_md: Graphical model for jointly Gaussian variables; zeros in the precision matrix encode conditional independence.
items.body_md: GGMs only handle continuous data, so discrete phenotype, condition and batch variables would have to be discarded. Neighbourhood selection (Meinshausen–Bühlmann) estimates the graph by regressing each node on the others with an L1 penalty.

items.gloss_md: Two variables are conditionally independent if, given all others, one carries no information about the other.
items.body_md: In a pairwise Markov random field, no edge between j and s means x_j ⊥ x_s | rest (Hammersley–Clifford / pairwise Markov property). In the regression view, the coefficient of x_s in the conditional mean of x_j is −β_js, so zero coupling equals zero regression coefficient.

items.gloss_md: Softmax model giving class probabilities from a linear predictor; the conditional of a discrete MGM node.
items.body_md: In the MGM, p(y_j = l | rest) is a softmax over states, with continuous features entering via ρ and other discrete features via φ. ADMIRE uses these probabilities to judge whether an observed label is plausible.

items.gloss_md: Per-cell score: standardized deviation from the conditional mean (continuous) or surprisal −log p (discrete).
items.body_md: For a continuous cell, s = |x − x̂|/√(β_jj⁻¹); the two-sided tail p = 2F(x̂ − ε) gives the same ranking. For a discrete cell with state k, s = −log p(k). Before computing x̂, suspect regressors (two-sided p < 5%) are replaced by group means or most probable states, making scores robust to co-occurring anomalies in one sample.

items.gloss_md: ADMIRE's threshold: compare sorted observed scores against scores of values simulated from the fitted conditionals.
items.body_md: For every cell a random value is drawn from its own conditional, giving an anomaly-free score set; observed and random scores are sorted and matched rank by rank (averaged over 100 draws). The threshold is the first rank where the random score exceeds the observed score. This self-calibrating null accounts for multiple testing and absorbs some model mis-specification, e.g. the heavier-than-Gaussian tails seen in real data.

items.gloss_md: Fitting on all samples but one and predicting the held-out sample, for each sample in turn.
items.body_md: ADMIRE fits one MGM per left-out sample so a sample's own anomalous value cannot pull its prediction toward itself. The same loop calibrates λ by minimizing reconstruction MSE over a penalty sequence, unlike the EBIC used by Altenbuchinger 2019.

items.gloss_md: Product of each node's conditional given all others, used instead of the full likelihood.
items.body_md: The full MGM density has an intractable normalising constant; the conditionals are closed-form, so the penalized negative pseudo log-likelihood is computationally feasible and consistent under regularity. ADMIRE minimizes it with proximal gradient descent, suited to the non-smooth L1 term; penalties are weighted per group/variance and features standardized.

items.gloss_md: Information criterion penalizing model complexity, used by Altenbuchinger 2019 to select the MGM penalty.
items.body_md: adadmire replaced EBIC by leave-one-out CV on reconstruction MSE, because its goal is accurate per-cell re-estimation rather than structure recovery.

items.gloss_md: Replacing flagged cells with their model re-estimates.
items.body_md: Even false positives do little harm, because a correct value's re-estimate is close to it anyway. In simulation MAPE dropped sharply; on the metabolomics data, correcting sample 7's anomalies cut MAPE vs validated values from 76.6 to 12.3. This makes ADMIRE usable as a preprocessing / normalisation step.

items.gloss_md: Filling in missing entries of a data matrix; ADMIRE uses a two-step MGM-based scheme.
items.body_md: Step 1: nearest-neighbour pre-imputation with Euclidean distance ignoring missing features. Step 2: fit an MGM on the completed data and re-estimate the missing cells from their conditionals. ADMIRE beat MissForest on continuous MAPE at 5–35% missingness and on discrete states in all settings; MissForest won above ~40%. MissForest is a non-parametric random-forest imputer for mixed data.

items.gloss_md: RPPA data of 77 proteins in mice with genotype, treatment and behaviour labels; ADMIRE's simulation basis.
items.body_md: After dropping proteins with missing values and subsampling: 400 samples × 68 continuous features plus 3 discrete features (8 groups of 50); log-transformed. Artificial anomalies shift min–max-scaled values by ε × a random amount; ε < 1 tends to give hidden anomalies, discrete anomalies swap states. The data contain intrinsic anomalies (~1,031 cells flagged without perturbation) from RPPA artefacts, counted as false positives and deflating precision.

items.gloss_md: Density-based k-NN anomaly score comparing a point's local density to its neighbours'.
items.body_md: A point in a much sparser region than its neighbours (LOF ≫ 1) is a local outlier. As a sample-level method it had to be applied feature by feature in the ADMIRE benchmark and trailed ADMIRE.

items.gloss_md: Search and TRace AnomalY: k-NN distance method thresholded via extreme-value theory.
items.body_md: It flags a point when the k-NN distance with the maximum gap is significantly large, modelling the tail of nearest-neighbour distances with a Gumbel domain of attraction. It was one of ADMIRE's three benchmark competitors.

items.gloss_md: Anomaly detector isolating points with random splits; anomalies have short average path lengths.
items.body_md: It uses no distance or density and runs in near-linear time. It was the best of ADMIRE's baselines, and its AUC rose when categorical variables were added via one-hot encoding, showing that phenotype conditioning matters.

items.gloss_md: Multi-source data-integration framework with pairwise MGMs from which adadmire's mgm.py descends.
items.body_md: It used a Lee & Hastie-style pairwise MGM with pseudo-likelihood, an L1 penalty and proximal-gradient fitting to learn conditional-independence networks across mixed molecular and clinical data, selecting the penalty by EBIC. It contained no anomaly detection at all.

items.gloss_md: A compound spiked at known amount into every sample; analytes are quantified by peak-area ratio to it.
items.body_md: It corrects for extraction losses, injection variability and ion suppression. Ideal internal standards are stable-isotope-labelled (¹³C, ¹⁵N, ²H) analogues that co-elute and ionise identically but differ in mass (isotope-dilution MS). A pipetting error in an internal-standard mix falsifies every metabolite quantified against it: the block of anomalies ADMIRE found in sample 7 (amino-acid method), confirmed by NMR, which uses a different reference (TSP).

items.gloss_md: Rapid, germline-encoded first line of defence without antigen-specific memory.
items.body_md: It detects PAMPs and DAMPs with pattern-recognition receptors and acts within minutes to hours. Components: barriers, complement, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), dendritic cells, NK cells and innate lymphoid cells. Dendritic cells bridge it to adaptive immunity.

items.gloss_md: Slower, antigen-specific immunity of B and T lymphocytes that generates memory.
items.body_md: Receptors are created by somatic V(D)J recombination; B cells provide humoral immunity (antibodies), T cells (CD4 helper, CD8 cytotoxic) cell-mediated immunity. Clonal selection expands antigen-specific clones over days.

items.gloss_md: Germline-encoded receptor (e.g. TLRs, NLRs, RIG-I-like receptors) sensing PAMPs and DAMPs.
items.body_md: PRRs give innate immunity its fixed recognition repertoire. Their engagement also upregulates costimulatory B7 on antigen-presenting cells, certifying a context of danger for T-cell activation.

items.gloss_md: Endosomal PRR that recognises unmethylated CpG DNA.
items.body_md: Unmethylated CpG is common in bacterial and viral genomes but rare in vertebrate DNA, so it is a PAMP. In humans TLR9 is expressed in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells and signals via MyD88 → IRAK → TRAF6 → NF-κB and IRF7. In B cells it promotes activation, proliferation, survival and antibody production; CpG was a stimulus of the P493/6 cultures.

items.gloss_md: Membrane immunoglobulin of B cells; crosslinking by antigen triggers BCR signalling.
items.body_md: Anti-IgM crosslinking mimics antigen engagement: Lyn/Syk, Igα/Igβ ITAM phosphorylation, the BLNK signalosome, PLCγ2, PI3K, Ca²⁺ flux and NF-κB, NFAT and MAPK pathways. Outcomes range from proliferation to anergy or apoptosis. F(ab)₂ fragments crosslink the BCR but lack Fc, avoiding inhibitory FcγRIIB signals.

items.gloss_md: Y-shaped protein of two heavy and two light chains; Fab binds antigen, Fc determines effector function.
items.body_md: V domains with hypervariable CDR loops form the antigen-binding sites; the heavy-chain constant region sets the isotype. IgM: first, pentameric, strong complement activator; IgG: main serum isotype, opsonisation, crosses placenta; IgA: mucosal; IgE: mast cells, allergy and parasites; IgD: naive B-cell BCR.

items.gloss_md: T-cell help signal: CD40L (CD154) on activated CD4⁺ T cells engages CD40 on B cells.
items.body_md: CD40 ligation recruits TRAFs and activates NF-κB and MAPK/JNK, driving B-cell survival, proliferation, germinal-centre formation, class switching (inducing AID) and affinity maturation. Loss of CD40L or CD40 causes Hyper-IgM syndrome. Soluble CD40L modelled T-help input in the P493/6 experiment.

items.gloss_md: Prototypical anti-inflammatory, immunoregulatory cytokine signalling via JAK1/TYK2–STAT3.
items.body_md: Produced by Tregs, Bregs, Th2 cells and macrophages, it suppresses TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-12 and downregulates MHC II and costimulation. On B cells it supports survival, proliferation and differentiation. In tumours it fosters an immunosuppressive microenvironment and can be a growth factor for lymphoma B cells.

items.gloss_md: Insulin-related growth factor signalling via the IGF-1R receptor tyrosine kinase.
items.body_md: It activates PI3K–AKT–mTOR and RAS–MAPK, supporting survival, proliferation and anabolic metabolism. Not a classical immune cytokine, it was a microenvironmental stimulus for the lymphoma B cells.

items.gloss_md: Master transcription-factor oncogene driving growth, proliferation and anabolic metabolism.
items.body_md: Deregulated MYC is a hallmark of B-cell lymphomas, e.g. the t(8;14) MYC–IgH translocation in Burkitt lymphoma. Metabolically it upregulates glycolysis, glutaminolysis, nucleotide and amino-acid synthesis and polyamine synthesis (ODC). In ADMIRE's metabolomics application MYC status (high/low) was a discrete feature.

items.gloss_md: EBV-immortalised human B cells with a tet-off conditional MYC transgene.
items.body_md: Doxycycline represses MYC (MYC-low); without it MYC is high. Experiments ran without estrogen, so the EBNA2 program was off and proliferation was MYC-driven. Cells were stimulated with microenvironmental factors (α-IgM, CD40L, CpG, IL-10, IGF-1), and supernatant metabolites were profiled by NMR (11) and MS (38) for 100 samples.

items.gloss_md: Malignancies of B cells, mostly of germinal-centre or post-GC origin.
items.body_md: AID-driven editing and rapid proliferation in germinal centres predispose to translocations (MYC–IgH in Burkitt, BCL2/BCL6 rearrangements). EBV is causally linked to several B-cell lymphomas (endemic Burkitt, some DLBCL, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease).

items.gloss_md: Follicular B-cell response with proliferation, AID-driven somatic hypermutation and class-switch recombination.
items.body_md: Germinal centres have a dark zone (proliferation and mutation) and a light zone (selection by Tfh help and antigen on follicular dendritic cells). AID initiates both somatic hypermutation (affinity maturation) and class-switch recombination (IgM → IgG/IgA/IgE). Off-target AID activity and DNA breaks make the GC a source of lymphoma translocations.

items.gloss_md: Major tryptophan-catabolism route (~95%), from tryptophan via kynurenine to quinolinic acid/NAD⁺.
items.body_md: IDO1/IDO2 or TDO oxidise tryptophan to N-formylkynurenine; kynurenine is further metabolised to 3-hydroxykynurenine, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid and quinolinic acid, with a branch to kynurenic and xanthurenic acid. It is immunosuppressive through tryptophan depletion and through kynurenine activating AhR. The minor serotonin branch (TPH → 5-hydroxytryptophan → serotonin → melatonin) competes for the same substrate.

items.gloss_md: IFN-γ-inducible enzyme catalysing the rate-limiting step of the kynurenine pathway.
items.body_md: IDO-mediated tryptophan depletion arrests effector T cells (sensed via GCN2/mTOR), and kynurenine promotes Tregs and tolerogenic dendritic cells via AhR. The IDO–kynurenine axis is a central mechanism of peripheral tolerance and tumour immune evasion, and a drug target.

items.gloss_md: Ligand-activated transcription factor sensing xenobiotics and endogenous ligands such as kynurenine.
items.body_md: On ligand binding it translocates to the nucleus and dimerises with ARNT. It promotes Treg differentiation, IL-22/Th17-related responses and tolerogenic dendritic cells, so the kynurenine → AhR axis is an immunosuppressive circuit exploited by tumours.

items.gloss_md: Pathway linking SAM (methyl donor) to putrescine, spermidine and spermine, with MTA as by-product.
items.body_md: Methionine + ATP gives SAM; decarboxylated SAM donates aminopropyl groups to make spermidine and spermine from putrescine (made from ornithine by ODC), releasing MTA, which is salvaged to methionine. Polyamines stabilise nucleic acids and support translation (spermidine for eIF5A hypusination) and are essential for proliferation. MYC upregulates ODC; polyamines are readouts of the proliferative state.

items.gloss_md: Molecule on all nucleated cells presenting endogenous peptides to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells.
items.body_md: Cytosolic peptides (8–10 aa) are made by the proteasome and transported into the ER by TAP; CD8 binds the α3 domain. This lets the immune system survey a cell's internal state; loss of MHC I licenses NK-cell killing ('missing self').

items.gloss_md: Molecule on professional APCs presenting exogenous peptides to CD4⁺ helper T cells.
items.body_md: Endocytosed proteins are degraded in the endosomal/lysosomal pathway; the invariant chain and HLA-DM manage loading of ~13–25 aa peptides; CD4 binds the β2 domain. Mnemonic: CD8 × MHC-I = 8; CD4 × MHC-II = 8.

items.gloss_md: Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg and Tfh subsets defined by driving cytokines, master transcription factors and outputs.
items.body_md: Th1 (T-bet): IFN-γ, intracellular pathogens. Th2 (GATA3): IL-4/5/13, helminths, allergy. Th17 (RORγt): IL-17/IL-22, extracellular bacteria and fungi. Treg (FoxP3): IL-10, TGF-β, tolerance. Tfh (Bcl-6): CD40L and IL-21 for germinal-centre B cells. The subsets cross-regulate.

items.gloss_md: Suppressive CD4⁺ CD25-high T cell defined by the master transcription factor FoxP3.
items.body_md: FoxP3 mutations cause the IPEX autoimmune syndrome. Tregs depend on IL-2 from other cells and suppress via IL-2 consumption, IL-10/TGF-β/IL-35, CTLA-4 stripping CD80/CD86, adenosine and cytolysis. They maintain peripheral tolerance but are co-opted by tumours.

items.gloss_md: Immunosuppressive B-cell functional state whose hallmark is IL-10 production.
items.body_md: Bregs suppress effector T-cell and dendritic-cell responses and promote Tregs. They are induced by TLR (CpG), CD40, BCR and inflammatory signals, the same stimuli applied to P493/6 cells, and can contribute to tumour immunosuppression.

items.gloss_md: Mechanisms preventing immune attack on self: central (thymus, bone marrow) and peripheral.
items.body_md: Central: thymic negative selection, with AIRE-driven expression of tissue antigens; B-cell deletion, receptor editing and anergy in the bone marrow. Peripheral: anergy, activation-induced cell death, Treg suppression, ignorance and checkpoint receptors (CTLA-4, PD-1). Failure causes autoimmunity; tumours exploit peripheral tolerance (PD-L1, Tregs, IDO).

items.gloss_md: Signal 1 TCR–peptide-MHC, signal 2 CD28–B7 costimulation, signal 3 polarising cytokines.
items.body_md: B7 is upregulated on APCs only after sensing danger, so costimulation certifies a real threat. Signal 1 without signal 2 leads to anergy or deletion, a peripheral-tolerance mechanism. CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7; this logic underlies checkpoint blockade.

items.gloss_md: How metabolic programs instruct immune-cell fate and function.
items.body_md: Naive T cells rely on OXPHOS and fatty-acid oxidation; effector T cells switch to aerobic glycolysis and glutaminolysis (PI3K–AKT–mTOR and MYC); memory T cells and Tregs favour fatty-acid oxidation/OXPHOS. M1 macrophages favour glycolysis and iNOS, M2 OXPHOS and arginase. Proliferating immune and tumour cells converge on glycolysis, glutaminolysis and biosynthesis, which metabolomic profiling reads out.

items.gloss_md: Cytosolic complex (e.g. NLRP3 + ASC + pro-caspase-1) that matures IL-1β and IL-18.
items.body_md: Signal 1 (priming via PRR/NF-κB) induces pro-IL-1β and NLRP3; signal 2 (ATP, crystals, toxins, ion flux) triggers assembly. Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and gasdermin D, whose pores release IL-1β and often cause pyroptosis. IL-1β lacks a signal peptide, so its release is gated by proteolysis and pore formation.

items.gloss_md: Canonical cytokine signalling: receptor-associated JAKs phosphorylate STAT transcription factors.
items.body_md: Ligand binding brings JAKs together to trans-phosphorylate each other and the receptor tail; STATs dock via SH2 domains, are phosphorylated, dimerise and enter the nucleus. Examples: IL-10R → JAK1/TYK2 → STAT3; IFN-γ → JAK1/2 → STAT1; IL-4 → STAT6. SOCS proteins give negative feedback; JAK inhibitors are used clinically.

items.gloss_md: Spectrum between proinflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory, pro-repair M2 macrophage states.
items.body_md: M1 (IFN-γ + LPS/TNF): TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-12, iNOS/NO, glycolysis. M2 (IL-4/IL-13, IL-10, TGF-β): arginase-1, OXPHOS, repair and angiogenesis. Tumour-associated macrophages are usually M2-like, immunosuppressive and associated with poor prognosis.

items.gloss_md: Cascade of ~30 proteins activated by classical, lectin and alternative pathways converging on C3.
items.body_md: Classical: C1q binds antibody; lectin: MBL/ficolins bind microbial sugars; alternative: spontaneous C3 tickover with an amplification loop. Effectors: opsonisation by C3b, anaphylatoxins C3a/C5a and the membrane attack complex C5b-9. Regulators (CD55, CD59, factor H, C1-INH) protect host cells.

items.gloss_md: Innate cytotoxic lymphocyte that kills based on balance of activating and inhibitory receptors.
items.body_md: Inhibitory receptors (KIRs, NKG2A) recognise self MHC I; cells losing MHC I ('missing self') or expressing stress ligands like MICA/B for NKG2D ('induced self') are killed with perforin and granzymes. NK cells complement CD8 T cells, catching tumours that escape them by losing MHC I.

items.gloss_md: Early alarm cytokines of acute inflammation such as TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8 and IFN-γ.
items.body_md: TNF-α activates endothelium and can drive septic shock; IL-1β is an endogenous pyrogen; IL-6 induces acute-phase proteins and Th17 polarisation; chemokines like IL-8 recruit neutrophils; IFN-γ activates macrophages and induces IDO. They are counterbalanced by IL-10 and TGF-β.
